gloss: To teach someone over a long period, especially in a school or college.
examples: Public schools *educate* nearly fifty million American children.
She was *educated* at a small college in Vermont.
The campaign is *educating* parents about online safety.

transitivity: both — transitive (tutor a student in math), intransitive (she tutors on weekends)
gloss: To teach one student or a very small group, usually privately.
examples: He *tutors* high school students in chemistry.
She *tutored* me all through my senior year.
I have been *tutoring* since my first semester.

gloss: To advise and guide a less experienced person over a long time.
examples: Senior nurses *mentor* everyone who joins the unit.
She *mentored* three graduate students last year.
He has *mentored* dozens of young teachers.

transitivity: both — transitive (coach a debate team), intransitive (he coaches at the middle school)
gloss: To train a person or team, or prepare someone for a test or performance.
examples: She *coaches* students for the SAT every spring.
He *coached* debate for ten years.
They are *coaching* her through the interview.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *coaches*.

ru: обучать на дому, давать домашнее образование
transitivity: both — transitive (they homeschool their kids), intransitive (the family homeschools)
gloss: To teach your own children at home instead of sending them to school.
examples: They *homeschool* their three children.
She was *homeschooled* until ninth grade.
More families are *homeschooling* this year.
contrast: Written as one word in American English: *homeschool*, *homeschooled*.

transitivity: both — transitive (retrain the staff), intransitive (he retrained as a nurse)
gloss: To learn, or to teach someone, a new set of skills for different work.
examples: The company will *retrain* anyone whose job disappears.
She *retrained* as a math teacher at forty.
He is *retraining* for a job in health care.

gloss: To give someone the information they need before they do something.
examples: The coach *briefs* the team before every game.
We were *briefed* on the new grading policy.
She is *briefing* the substitute teacher now.
contrast: You *brief* someone **on** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (debrief the students), intransitive (we debrief every Friday)
gloss: To talk through what happened after a task, a lesson, or a test.
examples: The instructor *debriefs* the class after every simulation.
They *debriefed* us as soon as the exercise ended.
We spent an hour *debriefing* after the presentation.

gloss: To gradually put an attitude or a habit into someone's mind.
examples: Good teachers *instill* curiosity, not just facts.
Her father *instilled* a love of reading in her.
The program is *instilling* better study habits.
contrast: American *instill*, British *instil*; the l doubles before endings: *instilled*, *instilling*.

gloss: To pass knowledge or information on to other people.
examples: A lecture can *impart* facts but not judgment.
She *imparted* everything she knew about the trade.
He has *imparted* his method to a whole generation of teachers.

gloss: To explain something to someone so that they finally understand it.
examples: Maybe you can *enlighten* me about the new rules.
The lecture *enlightened* nobody.
She has *enlightened* us on how the system really works.

gloss: To make someone familiar with something new.
examples: The first week *acquaints* students with the library.
We *acquainted* ourselves with the rules before the exam.
He is *acquainting* the class with the lab equipment.
contrast: You *acquaint* someone **with** something.

gloss: To learn about something, or teach someone about it, until it feels familiar.
examples: Take an hour to *familiarize* yourself with the software.
She *familiarized* the new students with the campus.
We are *familiarizing* ourselves with the syllabus.
contrast: American *familiarize*, British *familiarise*. You *familiarize* someone **with** something.

gloss: To help someone get used to a new place or situation.
examples: A short video *orients* new students.
They *oriented* us on the first day of class.
I am still *orienting* myself in this building.
contrast: Americans write *orient*; the British often write *orientate*.

gloss: To be a clear example of something, or to show it by example.
examples: These two sentences *exemplify* the rule.
Her essay *exemplified* everything we had practiced.
He has *exemplified* the standard we expect from seniors.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *exemplifies*, *exemplified*, but *exemplifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To say something again so that it is understood.
examples: Let me *reiterate* the main point.
She *reiterated* the deadline twice.
He kept *reiterating* that the exam would be open book.

gloss: To give a test, or to carry out an official procedure.
examples: The state *administers* the reading test every spring.
A nurse *administered* the hearing screening.
They are *administering* the exam in the gym.

ru: следить за порядком на экзамене, быть наблюдателем
transitivity: both — transitive (proctor the final), intransitive (she proctors on Saturdays)
gloss: To watch over students while they take an exam.
examples: Two graduate students *proctor* the final.
She *proctored* the makeup exam last Saturday.
I am *proctoring* in room 12 tomorrow.
contrast: American *proctor*; the British say *invigilate*.

transitivity: both — transitive (differentiate the two sounds), intransitive (differentiate between them)
gloss: To see or show the difference between two things.
examples: Beginners cannot *differentiate* these two vowels.
She *differentiated* between fact and opinion.
The teacher is *differentiating* her lessons for three reading levels.
contrast: You *differentiate* **between** A and B, or *differentiate* A **from** B.

gloss: To add something extra to what is already there.
examples: Short videos *supplement* the textbook.
She *supplemented* the lecture with a handout.
He is *supplementing* his income by tutoring.
contrast: The verb ends in a full *-ment*: SUP-luh-ment. The noun *a supplement* ends weakly: SUP-luh-muhnt.

gloss: To make something easier, or to lead a discussion or workshop.
examples: Small classes *facilitate* real discussion.
She *facilitated* the writing workshop last summer.
The grant has *facilitated* a new tutoring program.

transitivity: both — transitive (assist a student), intransitive (assist with the lab)
gloss: To help someone, especially with part of a task.
examples: Volunteers *assist* students with their homework.
She *assisted* the professor for two semesters.
He is *assisting* in the chemistry lab this year.
contrast: You *assist* someone **with** something, or *assist* **in** doing it.

transitivity: both — transitive (help your classmate), intransitive (she always helps)
gloss: To make it easier for someone to do something.
examples: Can you *help* me with these verbs?
She *helped* me study for the final.
He has *helped* dozens of students pass the exam.
contrast: After *help*, the bare infinitive is normal: *help me study* (also possible: *help me to study*).

gloss: To help something happen or work better.
examples: Pictures *aid* memory more than rereading does.
A quiet room *aided* her concentration.
Flashcards have *aided* thousands of language learners.

gloss: To encourage a skill, a feeling, or a habit to develop.
examples: Group projects *foster* cooperation.
That teacher *fostered* my interest in science.
The program has *fostered* real progress in reading.

gloss: To make someone more interested, active, or eager to think.
examples: Good questions *stimulate* thinking.
The film *stimulated* a long discussion.
The class is *stimulating* her interest in history.

transitivity: both — transitive (engage the class), intransitive (engage with the material)
gloss: To hold someone's interest, or to get seriously involved with something.
examples: A good lesson *engages* every student in the room.
She *engaged* the class with a story about her grandmother.
They are *engaging* more deeply with the text this year.
contrast: You *engage* **with** a text or a person; the -e drops before *-ing*: *engaging*.

gloss: To make someone lose confidence, or to try to stop them doing something.
examples: Harsh grading can *discourage* beginners.
A bad first semester *discouraged* him completely.
The school is *discouraging* students from taking five AP classes.
contrast: You *discourage* someone **from** doing something.

gloss: To tell someone officially that they have done something wrong.
examples: Teachers rarely *reprimand* a student in front of the class.
She was *reprimanded* for copying an essay.
The dean is *reprimanding* both of them this afternoon.

gloss: To make someone suffer a penalty for breaking a rule.
examples: Some teachers *punish* late work with a lower grade.
He was *punished* for cheating on the quiz.
They are *punishing* the whole class for one prank.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *punishes*. You *punish* someone **for** something.

gloss: To praise someone publicly or officially.
examples: The principal *commends* the students who improve the most.
She was *commended* for her research.
He has *commended* the class twice this month.
contrast: Not the same as *recommend*, which suggests rather than praises.

gloss: To forgive a small fault, or to officially let someone miss something.
examples: The office will *excuse* an absence with a note from home.
She *excused* him from gym class for a week.
You are *excused* from the final if your average is above 95.
contrast: The verb ends in a z sound (ik-SKYOOZ); the noun *an excuse* ends in s (ik-SKYOOS).

transitivity: both — transitive (enroll a child in school), intransitive (enroll in a course)
gloss: To officially join a school, a class, or a program.
examples: You can *enroll* in the course online.
She *enrolled* her son in a summer program.
Over four hundred students have *enrolled* this fall.
contrast: American *enroll*, British *enrol*; the l doubles: *enrolled*, *enrolling*. You *enroll* **in** a class.

transitivity: both — transitive (apply the rule), intransitive (apply to a college)
gloss: To ask formally to be accepted somewhere, or to put a rule or method to use.
examples: She wants to *apply* to three universities.
He *applied* for a scholarship in December.
We are *applying* what we learned last week.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *applies*, *applied*, but *applying* keeps the y. You *apply* **to** a school **for** a place.

gloss: To send in an application a second time.
examples: If they turn you down, you can *reapply* next year.
She *reapplied* in the fall and got in.
He is *reapplying* to the same program.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *reapplies*, *reapplied*, but *reapplying* keeps the y.

gloss: To put someone on a list of people waiting for a place.
examples: Popular seminars *waitlist* twenty or thirty students.
She was *waitlisted* at her first-choice college.
The registrar is *waitlisting* everyone who applied late.
contrast: Usually heard in the passive: *be waitlisted*.

gloss: To put something off until a later date.
examples: You may *defer* admission for one year.
He *deferred* his enrollment and worked abroad.
She is *deferring* the exam because of illness.
contrast: The stress is on the last syllable, so the r doubles: *deferred*, *deferring*.

transitivity: both — intransitive (she graduates in May), transitive (the school graduates 300 seniors a year)
gloss: To finish a course of study and receive a diploma or a degree.
examples: She will *graduate* in May.
He *graduated* from Ohio State in 2019.
Two hundred seniors are *graduating* this spring.
contrast: Americans *graduate* **from** a school. The verb is GRAJ-oo-ayt; the noun *a graduate* is GRAJ-oo-uht.

ru: получать квалификацию; давать право; проходить отбор
transitivity: both — transitive (the course qualifies you to teach), intransitive (she qualified as a nurse)
gloss: To reach the standard needed for a job, a place, or the next round.
examples: These two courses *qualify* you for the certificate.
She *qualified* as a nurse last year.
He is *qualifying* for the state finals.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *qualifies*, *qualified*, but *qualifying* keeps the y. You *qualify* **for** something or **as** something.

gloss: To study one subject as your main field at an American college.
examples: I want to *major* in linguistics.
She *majored* in biology.
He is *majoring* in computer science.
contrast: An American student *majors* **in** a subject; a British student simply *studies* it.

gloss: To concentrate on one narrow area of study or work.
examples: Doctors *specialize* after medical school.
She *specialized* in medieval history.
The school is *specializing* in the arts.
contrast: American *specialize*, British *specialise*. You *specialize* **in** something.

gloss: To officially recognize a school or program as meeting a standard.
examples: A regional board *accredits* the nursing program.
The state *accredited* the school in 2018.
They are *accrediting* the online degree this year.
contrast: Two c's but only one t: *accredited*, *accrediting*.

gloss: To work somewhere for a short time, often unpaid, in order to learn the job.
examples: Many students *intern* the summer before senior year.
She *interned* at a law firm in Chicago.
He is *interning* with a local newspaper.
contrast: The verb is stressed at the end (in-TURN); the noun *an intern* at the front (IN-turn).

ru: сопровождать (специалиста) для обучения, наблюдать за работой
gloss: To follow someone at work for a day or two in order to learn what the job is like.
examples: Juniors can *shadow* a nurse for a day.
He *shadowed* an engineer last spring.
She is *shadowing* a veterinarian this week.

gloss: To learn a trade by working under a skilled person.
examples: Young carpenters still *apprentice* under a master.
He *apprenticed* with a violin maker for four years.
She is *apprenticing* at a bakery this year.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-s* to the silent e: *apprentices*.

gloss: To go along with a group of young people in order to look after them.
examples: Parents *chaperone* every field trip.
My dad *chaperoned* the eighth-grade dance.
She is *chaperoning* the trip to Washington.
contrast: Also written *chaperon*, but *chaperone* is usual in American English.

transitivity: both — intransitive (cram for a test), transitive (cram three chapters into one night)
gloss: To study very hard in a short time just before a test.
examples: Try not to *cram* the night before the exam.
We *crammed* for six hours straight.
He is *cramming* for the chemistry final.
contrast: The m doubles: *crammed*, *cramming*. You *cram* **for** a test.

transitivity: both — transitive (prep the students), intransitive (prep for the test)
gloss: To get ready, or get someone ready, for something.
examples: I need to *prep* for tomorrow's quiz.
She *prepped* her students for the interview.
He is *prepping* for the bar exam.
contrast: The p doubles: *prepped*, *prepping*. Informal short form of *prepare*.

gloss: To keep something in your memory.
examples: Most people *retain* very little from a long lecture.
She *retained* almost everything she read.
He is *retaining* far more since he started using flashcards.

gloss: To learn something so thoroughly that it becomes automatic.
examples: Children *internalize* grammar rules without being taught them.
She had *internalized* her teacher's high standards.
You are *internalizing* the pattern every time you repeat it.
contrast: American *internalize*, British *internalise*.

gloss: To come back to a topic in order to look at it again.
examples: We will *revisit* this topic in chapter nine.
The class *revisited* the poem before the test.
I am *revisiting* my notes from last semester.

gloss: To improve a skill by practicing it carefully over time.
examples: Reading aloud every day *hones* your pronunciation.
She *honed* her writing in a summer workshop.
He has *honed* the technique over twenty years.
contrast: Drop the -e before *-ing*: *honing*.

gloss: To make what you have learned firmer, or to combine several things into one.
examples: A short review *consolidates* everything from the week.
Sleep *consolidated* the day's practice.
They are *consolidating* two classes into one.

gloss: To combine ideas from several sources into one whole.
examples: The essay asks you to *synthesize* three readings.
She *synthesized* the articles into a single argument.
They are *synthesizing* data from four studies.
contrast: American *synthesize*, British *synthesise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (generalize the rule), intransitive (try not to generalize)
gloss: To draw a broad conclusion from only a few cases.
examples: Learners often *generalize* a rule and use it where it does not fit.
He *generalized* from a single example.
She is *generalizing* about a whole country.
contrast: You *generalize* **from** evidence or **about** a group. American -ize, British -ise.

gloss: To connect one thing with another in your mind.
examples: Try to *associate* each new word with a picture.
She *associated* the smell of chalk with school.
I have always *associated* that book with my first teacher.
contrast: You *associate* one thing **with** another. The verb ends -ayt; the noun *an associate* ends -uht.

transitivity: both — transitive (relate the two ideas), intransitive (relate to a character)
gloss: To connect two things, or to understand and feel close to something.
examples: Good teaching *relates* new facts to what students already know.
She *related* the story to her own childhood.
I could not *relate* to that character at all.
contrast: *relate* **to** something means to understand it or feel connected to it.

gloss: To say that something was caused by or made by a particular person or thing.
examples: Students often *attribute* that quote to Mark Twain.
She *attributed* her success to one teacher.
He is *attributing* every bad grade to bad luck.
contrast: The verb is uh-TRIB-yoot; the noun *an attribute* is AT-ruh-byoot. You *attribute* something **to** someone.

transitivity: both — transitive (derive the formula), intransitive (the word derives from Latin)
gloss: To work something out from a starting point, or to come originally from a source.
examples: You can *derive* the whole formula from two simple rules.
The word *derived* from Latin.
We are *deriving* the equation step by step.
contrast: Something *derives* **from** a source; drop the -e before *-ing*: *deriving*.

gloss: To break a sentence into its grammatical parts, or to work out what a hard text means.
examples: First-year students *parse* Latin sentences every day.
I could not *parse* that question at all.
She is still *parsing* the instructions.

transitivity: both — transitive (search the index), intransitive (search for a source)
gloss: To look carefully for something.
examples: *Search* the index for the term.
I *searched* for an hour and found nothing.
She is *searching* the database for older studies.
contrast: You *search* **for** a thing, but you *search* a place: *search the library* means look through it.

transitivity: both — transitive (double-check your answers), intransitive (double-check before you submit)
gloss: To check something a second time to be sure it is right.
examples: *Double-check* your answers before you hand in the test.
She *double-checked* every calculation.
I am *double-checking* the spelling of his name.
contrast: Written with a hyphen: *double-check*, *double-checked*, *double-checking*.

gloss: To look at something again in order to judge it properly.
examples: Historians *reexamine* old evidence all the time.
She *reexamined* her notes after class.
We are *reexamining* the first three chapters.
contrast: American writing usually joins it up: *reexamine* (British *re-examine*).

gloss: To judge or measure something again, usually after new information.
examples: Teachers *reassess* every student at the end of the unit.
The school *reassessed* his reading level in March.
They are *reassessing* the whole curriculum.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *reassesses*.

gloss: To do a piece of work again in a different or better way.
examples: You may *rework* the essay for a higher grade.
She *reworked* the problem three times before it came out right.
He is *reworking* his introduction.

gloss: To repeat an experiment or a result exactly.
examples: Students *replicate* a famous experiment in week three.
No one could *replicate* her results.
They are *replicating* the study with older children.

gloss: To try something new in order to see what happens.
examples: We *experiment* with different study methods every term.
She *experimented* with flashcards for a month.
He is *experimenting* with teaching the whole class in Spanish.
contrast: You *experiment* **with** a method and *experiment* **on** a subject.

transitivity: both — transitive (hypothesize that sleep helps), intransitive (scientists hypothesize, then test)
gloss: To suggest an explanation that can then be tested.
examples: Scientists *hypothesize* first and test afterward.
She *hypothesized* that sleep improves recall.
We are *hypothesizing* about the cause.
contrast: American *hypothesize*, British *hypothesise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (theorize that the text had two authors), intransitive (theorize about the cause)
gloss: To form an idea about why something is as it is, without full proof.
examples: Historians still *theorize* about why the city fell.
He *theorized* that the text had two authors.
They are *theorizing* with very little evidence.

gloss: To prove that a statement or an argument is wrong.
examples: Your job in the debate is to *refute* the other side.
She *refuted* the claim in two sentences.
He has *refuted* every point so far.

gloss: To confuse someone completely.
examples: English spelling *perplexes* almost every learner.
The last question *perplexed* even the teacher.
The results have *perplexed* researchers for years.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *perplexes*.

gloss: To ask something so hard that the other person cannot answer.
examples: That riddle *stumps* everyone.
The last problem *stumped* me completely.
She has *stumped* the whole class with one question.

gloss: To take someone's attention away from what they are doing.
examples: Phones *distract* everyone in the room.
The noise *distracted* me during the whole exam.
She is *distracting* the entire back row.
contrast: You *distract* someone **from** their work.

gloss: To pay attention to a sound, a person, or a recording.
examples: *Listen* to the recording twice before you answer.
She *listened* to the lecture again at double speed.
I have been *listening* to podcasts to train my ear.
contrast: The t is silent. You *listen* **to** something — never listen the radio.

gloss: To put an idea into clear words, or to pronounce sounds clearly.
examples: Try to *articulate* exactly what you do not understand.
She *articulated* the problem better than the professor did.
He is learning to *articulate* his ideas in English.
contrast: The verb ends ar-TIK-yuh-layt; the adjective *articulate* ends ar-TIK-yuh-luht.

transitivity: both — transitive (enunciate each syllable), intransitive (enunciate clearly)
gloss: To pronounce words clearly and distinctly.
examples: *Enunciate* every syllable when you read aloud.
She *enunciated* each word for the beginners.
He is *enunciating* much better after a month of practice.

gloss: To say a word with the wrong sounds or the wrong stress.
examples: Almost everyone *mispronounces* my last name.
He *mispronounced* the word colonel in front of the whole class.
She is afraid of *mispronouncing* words out loud.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *mispronounces*.

gloss: To have a real conversation, especially in a foreign language.
examples: By May the class can *converse* in simple Spanish.
We *conversed* in French for an hour.
She is *conversing* with a native speaker twice a week.
contrast: The verb is kuhn-VURS; the noun *the converse* (the opposite) is KAHN-vurs. You *converse* **with** someone.

gloss: To match something else, or to exchange letters with someone.
examples: The numbers in the margin *correspond* to the notes at the back.
They *corresponded* for two years before they met.
She has been *corresponding* with a class in Japan.
contrast: A thing *corresponds* **to** another thing; a person *corresponds* **with** another person.

gloss: To pass a message or information on to someone else.
examples: Please *relay* the assignment to anyone who was absent.
She *relayed* the principal's message to the class.
He is *relaying* the questions to the speaker.
contrast: A vowel before -y keeps the y: *relays*, *relayed*, never relaid.

gloss: To describe something fully, point by point.
examples: The syllabus *details* every assignment.
She *detailed* her method in the appendix.
The handbook is *detailing* the new rules for next fall.
contrast: The verb is stressed at the end: di-TAYL. The noun *a detail* is usually DEE-tayl.

gloss: To watch a recording or a video again.
examples: You can *rewatch* the lecture as many times as you like.
She *rewatched* the lab demonstration twice.
He is *rewatching* last week's class before the quiz.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *rewatches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the change benefits everyone), intransitive (benefit from extra practice)
gloss: To gain an advantage from something, or to do someone good.
examples: Slower readers *benefit* from extra practice.
She *benefited* from a year abroad.
The whole class is *benefiting* from the smaller size.
contrast: American English keeps one t: *benefited*, *benefiting* (British often *benefitted*). You *benefit* **from** something.

gloss: To do what a rule, a promise, or a requirement asks for.
examples: Two lab courses *fulfill* the science requirement.
She *fulfilled* the language requirement with Spanish.
He is *fulfilling* his last credits this summer.
contrast: American *fulfill*, British *fulfil*; both double the l before endings: *fulfilled*, *fulfilling*.

gloss: To do what a rule or an order requires.
examples: All students must *comply* with the honor code.
The school *complied* with the new state rules.
They are *complying* fully with the policy.
contrast: You *comply* **with** a rule. Consonant + *-y* changes: *complies*, *complied*.

gloss: To act in a particular way, or to act properly.
examples: The kids *behave* better with a substitute than with me.
He *behaved* beautifully all semester.
They are *behaving* as if the test did not matter.
contrast: On its own, *behave* means behave well; with a reflexive it is stronger: *behave yourself*.

gloss: To act badly, especially in class.
examples: Two boys always *misbehave* in the back row.
She *misbehaved* only once all year.
He was sent to the office for *misbehaving*.

transitivity: both — intransitive (cheat on a test), transitive (cheat someone out of money)
gloss: To break the rules of a test or a game in order to gain an advantage.
examples: Nobody needs to *cheat* on a take-home exam.
He *cheated* on the final and was expelled.
She was caught *cheating* in the first week.
contrast: You *cheat* **on** a test and *cheat* **at** cards.

gloss: To keep going despite difficulty, or to continue to exist.
examples: Students who *persist* through the first year usually finish.
She *persisted* until the proof finally worked.
The problem is *persisting* into the second semester.
contrast: You *persist* **in** doing something, or *persist* **with** a task.

gloss: To keep trying at something hard for a long time.
examples: You have to *persevere* through the difficult chapters.
She *persevered* and finished the degree in five years.
He is *persevering* after two failed attempts.
contrast: Note the three e's: per-se-vere. You *persevere* **with** a task or **in** doing something.

gloss: To try to do something, especially something difficult.
examples: *Attempt* every question, even if you are unsure.
She *attempted* the bonus problem and got it right.
He is *attempting* the exam for the third time.
contrast: You *attempt* **to do** something, never attempt do something.

gloss: To start dealing with a difficult problem or task.
examples: *Tackle* the hardest question first.
She *tackled* the whole reading list over the summer.
We are *tackling* fractions this week.

gloss: To manage successfully with something difficult.
examples: Some freshmen cannot *cope* with the workload.
She *coped* well with a heavy schedule.
He is *coping* better since the tutoring started.
contrast: You *cope* **with** something; drop the -e before *-ing*: *coping*.

gloss: To achieve what you were trying to do.
examples: Students *succeed* when someone expects them to.
She *succeeded* on her second try.
He has *succeeded* in every class he has taken.
contrast: You *succeed* **in** doing something, or *succeed* **at** a subject.

gloss: To be extremely good at something.
examples: She *excels* at languages.
He *excelled* in math but struggled with writing.
They are *excelling* in the new program.
contrast: The l doubles: *excelled*, *excelling*. You *excel* **at** or **in** something.

gloss: To do better than someone or something else.
examples: Small classes usually *outperform* large ones.
She *outperformed* every student in her year.
The new method is *outperforming* the old one.

gloss: To go beyond someone or something in quality or amount.
examples: Her essay *surpasses* anything else in the class.
He *surpassed* his own record on the third try.
The results have *surpassed* what anyone expected.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *surpasses*.

gloss: To try to win or to do better than others.
examples: Ten schools *compete* in the spelling bee.
She *competed* in the science fair twice.
They are *competing* for two scholarships.
contrast: You *compete* **with** or **against** someone **for** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (flunk chemistry), intransitive (half the class flunked)
gloss: To fail a test or a course, or to give someone a failing grade.
examples: If you skip the final, you *flunk* the course.
He *flunked* chemistry and had to take it again.
She is *flunking* two classes this semester.
contrast: Informal American English for *fail*.

gloss: To do extremely well on a test or in an interview.
examples: If you study tonight, you will *ace* this quiz.
She *aced* the interview.
He has *aced* every test so far this year.
contrast: Drop the -e before *-ing*: *acing*. Informal American English.

gloss: To take an active part in something.
examples: Part of your grade is how often you *participate*.
She *participated* in every discussion.
Only half the class is *participating* today.
contrast: You *participate* **in** something.

gloss: To work together with someone toward the same goal.
examples: The two schools *cooperate* on a summer program.
He *cooperated* fully with the investigation.
They are *cooperating* on a joint project.
contrast: Americans write *cooperate* without a hyphen (British often *co-operate*). You *cooperate* **with** someone **on** something.

gloss: To join with another person or group in order to work together.
examples: *Partner* with someone you have not worked with yet.
She *partnered* with a classmate for the lab report.
Our school is *partnering* with a community college.
contrast: You *partner* **with** someone.

gloss: To spend time with other people in a friendly way.
examples: Freshmen mostly *socialize* in the dorms.
We *socialized* for an hour after the exam.
She is *socializing* much more this year.
contrast: American *socialize*, British *socialise*.

gloss: To become a friend to someone, especially someone new or alone.
examples: Older students *befriend* the newcomers in September.
She *befriended* a girl from Brazil.
He has *befriended* everyone on his floor.

gloss: To be owned by someone, or to feel accepted in a place.
examples: This textbook *belongs* to the library.
She never felt she *belonged* at that school.
Children learn better when they feel they *belong*.
contrast: *belong* **to** someone means it is theirs; with no preposition it means being in the right place.

transitivity: both — transitive (acclimate the new students), intransitive (acclimate to college)
gloss: To get used to a new place, climate, or situation.
examples: It takes about a month to *acclimate* to college.
She *acclimated* quickly to the new school.
He is still *acclimating* to classes taught in English.
contrast: Americans say *acclimate*; the British say *acclimatize*. You *acclimate* **to** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (count the pages), intransitive (this quiz counts)
gloss: To say numbers in order or find a total, or to matter toward a result.
examples: First graders *count* to a hundred by tens.
She *counted* the votes twice.
I am *counting* the days until graduation.

gloss: To take one number away from another.
examples: *Subtract* seven from twelve.
The teacher *subtracted* five points for turning it in late.
We are *subtracting* fractions this week.
contrast: You *subtract* one number **from** another.

gloss: To change a number to the nearest simpler one.
examples: *Round* your answer to two decimal places.
She *rounded* 4.6 up to 5.
The program is *rounding* every score to the nearest whole number.
contrast: You *round* a number **to** the nearest ten, and *round* it up or down.

ru: усреднять, выводить среднее; составлять в среднем
gloss: To find the middle value of several numbers, or to reach that value typically.
examples: The teacher *averages* your four best quizzes.
He *averaged* a B plus for the semester.
She is *averaging* two hours of homework a night.

transitivity: both — transitive (tally the votes), intransitive (the two lists tally)
gloss: To count things up, or for two sets of numbers to match.
examples: *Tally* the votes on the board.
She *tallied* the scores after the quiz.
We are *tallying* the results now.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *tallies*, *tallied*, but *tallying* keeps the y.

gloss: To work a number out again.
examples: *Recalculate* the average without the lowest score.
He *recalculated* his grade three times.
She is *recalculating* the totals after the correction.

gloss: To come close to a value, or to estimate it roughly.
examples: You can *approximate* the answer before you do the arithmetic.
She *approximated* the cost in her head.
The model is *approximating* real conditions fairly well.
contrast: The verb ends uh-PRAHK-suh-mayt; the adjective *approximate* ends -suh-muht.

transitivity: both — transitive (substitute the value of x), intransitive (substitute for a teacher)
gloss: To put one thing in place of another, or to take someone's place for a while.
examples: *Substitute* the value of x in the equation.
She *substituted* for our teacher all last week.
He is *substituting* at the middle school this year.
contrast: You *substitute* A **for** B, and you *substitute* **for** the person whose place you take.

gloss: To draw a set of numbers as a line or a curve on axes.
examples: Today we *graph* linear equations.
She *graphed* the results on the board.
They are *graphing* the data by hand.

gloss: To record progress or information in a table or a diagram.
examples: Teachers *chart* each student's progress every month.
We *charted* the class's reading speed all year.
She is *charting* her study hours in a notebook.

gloss: To draw something as a diagram, especially the parts of a sentence.
examples: American students still *diagram* sentences in grammar class.
She *diagrammed* the water cycle on the board.
He is *diagramming* the argument step by step.
contrast: The m usually doubles: *diagrammed*, *diagramming*.

gloss: To arrange things in the right order.
examples: Second graders *sequence* the events of a story.
She *sequenced* the lessons so that the hardest came last.
We are *sequencing* the units differently this year.
contrast: Drop the -e before *-ing*: *sequencing*.

ru: повышать оценки по кривой (о шкале оценок)
gloss: To raise a whole class's grades against a scale.
examples: Professors sometimes *curve* a very hard exam.
She *curved* the midterm by eight points.
He is *curving* the final grades this semester.
contrast: In American schools, to *curve* a test means to adjust everyone's score, usually upward.
